source_trace: Diagnostic Portfolio Master Library — DRIVE (SHIFT portfolio)
meta.naming_note: The canonical instrument name is DRIVE (no version suffix). The engine internally references v2 but the product name is simply DRIVE. See DRIVE naming rule in memory.

identity.name: DRIVE
identity.tagline: Know what fuels you. Know what fades you.
identity.description: A 36-item motivational assessment with 30 core motivation items and 6 engagement risk items. DRIVE measures motivation architecture across five dimensions (Intrinsic Motivation, Extrinsic Motivation, Values Alignment, Confidence & Self-Efficacy, Growth Orientation) and classifies individuals into 10 motivational profiles across three engagement states (Fueled, Flickering, Fading).
identity.ideal_use_case: Leadership development and coaching intake; career transition assessment; team motivational mapping; engagement risk identification for high-potential leaders; pre-hire motivational fit evaluation.

instrument_spec.delivery_format: Online self-assessment with instant HTML report
instrument_spec.scoring_method: 5 dimension normalised scores (0–20 each) + composite 0–100 + engagement risk sub-score (Fueled/Flickering/Fading)

dimensions.name: Intrinsic Motivation
dimensions.description: Measures the degree to which the individual is motivated by the inherent satisfaction of the work itself — curiosity, craft, autonomy, and flow — rather than external rewards or recognition.
dimensions.what_high_means: The individual finds deep satisfaction in the work itself, experiences flow regularly, is driven by curiosity and mastery, and works effectively with autonomy.
dimensions.what_low_means: The individual is not primarily motivated by the inherent nature of the work; relies more on external factors to sustain engagement.

dimensions.name: Extrinsic Motivation
dimensions.description: Measures the degree to which the individual is motivated by external rewards, recognition, status, visibility, and career progression.
dimensions.what_high_means: The individual is strongly motivated by recognition, rewards, visibility, and advancement; these factors drive sustained effort and performance.
dimensions.what_low_means: The individual is less responsive to external rewards and recognition; may be self-driven or may lack clarity about how to achieve recognition.

dimensions.name: Values Alignment
dimensions.description: Measures the degree of alignment between the individual's personal values, sense of purpose, and the organisation's mission and ethics.
dimensions.what_high_means: The individual feels their work is meaningfully aligned with their values and purpose; they can articulate their values clearly and feel the organisation's ethics are compatible with their own.
dimensions.what_low_means: The individual experiences values conflict with their role or organisation; purpose congruence is low; sustained engagement based on values is unlikely.

dimensions.name: Confidence & Self-Efficacy
dimensions.description: Measures the individual's belief in their own capability to succeed in their role — including confidence under pressure, ability to adapt, and conviction in their own skills.
dimensions.what_high_means: The individual has strong confidence in their capabilities, performs well under pressure, adapts their approach effectively, and believes they can handle challenges.
dimensions.what_low_means: The individual doubts their capabilities, especially under pressure; may struggle with confidence in new or challenging contexts.

dimensions.name: Growth Orientation
dimensions.description: Measures the degree to which the individual is motivated by growth, development, learning, and new challenges — versus mastery, stability, and doing what they already do well.
dimensions.what_high_means: The individual is driven by new challenges and development opportunities; actively seeks learning; prefers steep learning curves; has strong growth appetite in APAC contexts.
dimensions.what_low_means: The individual prefers mastery and stability over development; may be less motivated in roles requiring continuous new learning; growth pace in APAC may feel overwhelming.

states.description: The individual is sustainably engaged; motivation architecture supports current role demands.
Engagement is inconsistent; some motivational dimensions are not being met; intervention can prevent further decline.
Significant disengagement risk; motivational architecture is structurally misaligned with role; active intervention required.

archetype_framework.logic: Archetypes are determined by dominant motivation type (Intrinsic, Extrinsic, Purpose-driven, Growth-driven, Dual-drive, or Depleted/Blocked) combined with engagement state (Fueled, Flickering, Fading). Primary classification uses D1 vs D2 dominance, with D3 (Values) and D5 (Growth) as override conditions.

motivation_type_rules.step1: If |D1-D2| >= threshold → Intrinsic or Extrinsic dominant. If < threshold → Dual-drive.
motivation_type_rules.step2: If D3 > both D1 and D2 → Purpose-driven override. If D5 > both D1 and D2 → Growth-driven override.
motivation_type_rules.step3: If no clear dominant across D1/D2/D3/D5 → Drifter flag.

archetypes.name: Achiever
archetypes.core_description: The Achiever is driven by recognition, progression, and visible results. They set ambitious targets, seek advancement, and thrive when their contributions are acknowledged and rewarded.
strengths: Results-oriented and high-output
Strong drive for progression and visibility
High confidence in their capabilities
Growth-oriented — actively develops for advancement
growth_areas: Risk of burning out when recognition dries up
May prioritise visible wins over deeper, less visible value creation
Intrinsic motivation may be thinner than it appears
Vulnerable to environments with unclear reward structures
archetypes.development_focus: Strengthen intrinsic motivation for sustainable engagement; develop appreciation for non-visible value creation; build recognition-independent performance standards.

archetypes.name: Craftsman
archetypes.pattern: Motivated by excellence of the work
archetypes.core_description: The Craftsman is deeply motivated by the quality and craft of the work itself. They find satisfaction in doing work well, in mastery of their discipline, and in alignment between their values and their work.
strengths: Deep work satisfaction independent of external rewards
Commitment to quality and craftsmanship
Strong values alignment with their work
Sustainable engagement through intrinsic satisfaction
growth_areas: May be demotivated by bureaucracy and mediocrity
Can be slow to advance because less driven by visibility and recognition
May undervalue their own commercial impact
Risk of becoming complacent in stable environments
archetypes.development_focus: Build external orientation — stakeholder visibility, commercial impact awareness; develop career advancement strategy aligned with intrinsic values; practice communicating value in ways that resonate with extrinsic systems.

archetypes.name: Champion
archetypes.core_description: The Champion is energised by developing others and building team capability. They thrive when they can see their impact through the growth and success of people around them, and they are driven by the recognition and visibility that comes from team achievements.
strengths: Strong people development orientation
High confidence that inspires others
Growth-oriented — both for self and team
Recognition from team success fuels sustained effort
growth_areas: Loses motivation when team structure changes or team is removed
May prioritise team harmony over individual performance standards
Risk of over-investing in low-potential team members
Personal identity may be too tied to team role
archetypes.development_focus: Build independent motivational foundations not solely dependent on team role; develop individual performance management capability; practice maintaining motivation during team transitions.

archetypes.name: Explorer
archetypes.pattern: Driven by new challenges and contexts
archetypes.core_description: The Explorer is motivated by novelty, challenge, and new contexts. They thrive on steep learning curves, new environments, and the excitement of figuring things out. Their motivation waxes and wanes with the novelty curve.
strengths: Thrives in new and challenging situations
Rapid learning capability
Comfortable with ambiguity and change
Strong growth orientation
growth_areas: Disengages in stable, routine mandates
May move on before mastering or seeing through long-term initiatives
Risk of breadth without depth
Can become restless in roles with long plateau phases
archetypes.development_focus: Build stamina for the mastery phase of roles; develop satisfaction from deepening expertise rather than just new challenges; identify how to bring exploratory energy to stable contexts.

archetypes.name: Stalwart
archetypes.core_description: The Stalwart is anchored in strong values alignment and intrinsic motivation, with lower growth orientation. They are loyal, steady, and deeply committed to the mission and purpose of the organisation. They are the durable backbone of institutional knowledge and culture.
strengths: Deep institutional loyalty and commitment
Strong values alignment with the organisation
Reliable and consistent over long periods
Custodians of organisational culture and knowledge
growth_areas: Can be rigid in changing contexts
Lower growth orientation may mean slower adaptation to new requirements
May resist organisational change that disrupts familiar patterns
Risk of becoming outdated if development needs accelerate
archetypes.development_focus: Build openness to change and growth; develop adaptive capacity for shifting contexts; connect growth and development to values and purpose rather than seeing it as disruption.

archetypes.name: Restless
archetypes.core_description: The Restless has strong capability and high ambition (high extrinsic + growth orientation) but feels misaligned with the role's purpose or values. They are capable but not fully engaged — the role doesn't stretch or fulfil them enough to sustain full motivation.
strengths: High capability and ambition
Strong growth orientation
Driven by progression and recognition
Clear about what they want — advancement
growth_areas: Will exit if mandate does not expand or values alignment does not improve
May disengage incrementally — still performing but not at full capacity
Risk of looking for opportunities externally before internal options are exhausted
Values misalignment creates background dissatisfaction that affects long-term retention
archetypes.development_focus: Clarify values alignment gap — is it role-specific or organisational? Explore growth opportunities that increase values congruence; assess whether role scope can expand to match capability and ambition.

archetypes.name: Golden Handcuffs
archetypes.pattern: Staying for rewards, not the work
archetypes.core_description: The Golden Handcuffs profile stays primarily for the rewards and compensation (high extrinsic) and because the role's values are acceptable (moderate-high values alignment), but finds little intrinsic satisfaction in the work itself. They are reliable but not energised.
strengths: Reliable performer — will meet expectations
Values alignment prevents active disengagement
Understands the reward system and works within it effectively
Stable presence in the organisation
growth_areas: Explore what would need to change to re-engage intrinsic motivation
Risk of prolonged mediocre performance — showing up but not contributing at full capacity
May stay far longer than is healthy for their development
Vulnerable to being passed over for more visibly motivated peers
archetypes.development_focus: Identify what would re-engage intrinsic motivation — is it role content, autonomy, challenge, or something else? Assess whether staying is serving long-term career interests or just short-term comfort.

archetypes.name: Drifter
archetypes.core_description: The Drifter lacks a clear dominant motivation source. They are not strongly driven by intrinsic satisfaction, external rewards, purpose alignment, or growth. Work feels arbitrary and engagement is inconsistent — some days are fine, others feel pointless.
strengths: Often capable — the issue is motivation, not ability
May be in a transition period between motivational phases
Flexible — not locked into one motivational pattern
Open to discovering what drives them
growth_areas: Mandates feel arbitrary and unmoored from personal motivation
Performance is unpredictable — dependent on whether the work happens to engage them
Risk of prolonged underperformance without intervention
May not have developed self-awareness about what actually motivates them
archetypes.development_focus: Conduct systematic motivational exploration — test different types of work, goals, and rewards to identify what creates sustained engagement; work with a coach to develop motivational self-awareness.

archetypes.name: Burned-Out
archetypes.core_description: The Burned-Out profile shows structural depletion across intrinsic motivation, confidence, and growth orientation. The individual has lost belief in their own capability, no longer finds satisfaction in the work, and has stopped seeking growth. This is a serious engagement state requiring immediate attention.
strengths: Often were high performers before depletion set in
Recovery is possible with the right intervention
Typically have deep capability and institutional knowledge
Recovery often leads to renewed clarity about what matters
growth_areas: Immediate safety assessment required — risk of further deterioration
Confidence collapse affects both performance and help-seeking
Intrinsic motivation depletion means the work itself no longer provides reward
Growth orientation collapse means they cannot imagine things getting better
archetypes.development_focus: Immediate intervention: workload assessment, burnout recovery plan, possible role change or sabbatical. Focus on safety and recovery first, then rebuilding motivation. Professional support (therapy, coaching) is strongly indicated.

archetypes.name: Frozen Asset
archetypes.core_description: The Frozen Asset has strong values alignment — they believe in the organisation and its mission — but low confidence and low growth orientation have led to a state of structural paralysis. They are capable but stuck, neither growing nor contributing at their full potential.
strengths: Strong values alignment — genuinely committed to the organisation's mission
Often significant untapped capability beneath the paralysis
Loyal and stable — will not leave easily
Recovery can release substantial value for the organisation
growth_areas: Organisational or mandate design intervention may be required
Low confidence creates self-reinforcing paralysis — less action, less confidence
Low growth orientation means they may not actively seek to change their situation
Risk of prolonged underutilisation, which gradually erodes capability further
archetypes.development_focus: Structural intervention — role redesign, mandate clarification, or targeted development programme. Build confidence through small wins and increasing autonomy. Connect growth opportunities to values alignment to increase motivation for change.

composite_scoring.method: Five-dimension average of normalised core scores, converted to 0–100 composite (engagement risk items scored separately)

bands.interpretation: Strong motivation across multiple dimensions; highly engaged and directed.
Generally energised; 1–2 motivation dimensions with meaningful gaps.
Partial alignment; significant gaps between role and motivational architecture.
Substantial misalignment; disengagement risk is material.
Motivational breakdown; urgent career review and role redesign required.

dimension_verdicts.meaning: Mature motivation architecture with sustainable engagement
Moderate motivation with identifiable risk factors
Significant motivation architecture gap requiring intervention

report_output.report_format: Interactive HTML report with visual motivation profile
